title: Good Gifts and Steady Leadership
overview: Paul warns Timothy about teachers who call good things like marriage and food off limits, and urges him to train in godliness and lead by example despite his youth.

parts.label: A warning about false teachers (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Early Christians believed they were already living in the 'later times', so Paul means teachers active in his own day, not only in some distant future. Their consciences are pictured as seared or branded with a hot iron, so dulled that they no longer feel the wrong they do while putting on a holy show.

parts.label: Food and marriage are good (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: These teachers banned marriage and certain foods as a path to holiness, though scholars are unsure exactly who they were. Paul answers with the creation story's claim that what God made is good, and says food is made holy by God's word and prayer, which may mean grace said in words drawn from Scripture or God's own declaration that creation is good.

parts.label: Training for godliness (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Paul borrows the picture of athletes in training: physical exercise helps a little, but training in godliness shapes all of life, now and after death. He calls God the Savior of all people and especially of believers, which readers take in different ways, either as God caring for everyone or as salvation offered to all and received by those who trust.

parts.label: Young but setting the example (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Timothy was probably young compared with the people he led, so Paul tells him to earn respect through how he speaks and lives. Reading Scripture aloud was central to early gatherings, and the elders laying their hands on him was a ceremony that commissioned him for his role, along with prophetic words about his calling.

parts.label: Keep watch and keep going (vv. 15-16)
parts.note: Paul wants Timothy's growth to be visible to everyone, and he ties together how Timothy lives and what he teaches. 'Save' here most likely means staying on the path of faith and helping his listeners stay on it too.

think: Where would you draw the line between self-discipline that genuinely makes a person better and rules that only make ordinary good things seem shameful?
